analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas drilling off the New England coast.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would permanently bar oil and gas leasing off the coasts of Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut, has 10 cosponsors including one Republican and has sat in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing or vote since April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a permanent prohibition into law: the Interior Secretary could never issue a lease for oil or gas exploration or production anywhere in the federal waters off Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, or Connecticut. It responds to recurring federal proposals to open the Atlantic to drilling, which New England's fishing, tourism, and coastal communities have opposed because a spill anywhere along the shared ocean would reach their waters. A current law cannot be changed by a future administration without Congress acting again, which is the point of making the ban statutory.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial fishing crews, and the tourism economies of the five New England states, who gain permanent protection from the risk of offshore spills and the industrial activity that accompanies drilling. The bill's sponsors say it protects a regional ocean economy worth billions and thousands of jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: New England fishing and coastal tourism towns

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production off Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, or Connecticut, and it says this overrides any other provision of law.

Because the ban is written into statute, no future administration could open these waters to drilling on its own the way leasing plans can otherwise be rewritten between presidencies; undoing it would require Congress to pass a new law.
The ban covers the entire New England outer Continental Shelf, the federal ocean waters beyond state lines that individual coastal states cannot protect on their own.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which lose the option of ever leasing and drilling in New England's federal waters. Taxpayers and consumers feel no direct cost; the region holds little known oil and gas potential, so the forgone production is likely small, and coastal communities that see drilling as a threat to fishing and tourism gain instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Atlantic leases

drawbacks.text: The ban forecloses any future domestic energy production in New England's federal waters, even if new discoveries or higher prices made drilling there economically worthwhile someday.

It removes a potential, though speculative, source of domestic oil and gas supply and federal royalty revenue, which supporters of expanded offshore drilling point to when arguing for opening new areas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and permanent, and the cost is largely hypothetical: the New England outer Continental Shelf has never been a significant oil and gas producer, while fishing and tourism are established regional employers that a spill would threaten. The main honest objection is that a permanent statutory ban forecloses options that a future Congress might want back, rather than leaving the decision to each administration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has not held a hearing or vote on it; it stays there unless the committee or the Senate acts.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, joined by nine original cosponsors: Sens. Blumenthal, Collins, Hassan, King, Markey, Murphy, Reed, Shaheen, and Warren, the full New England Senate delegation plus Sen. Collins of Maine.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which is the only action it has received.
Ten senators in total have cosponsored the bill, including 8 of the Senate's 45 Democrats, 1 of 55 Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has won or lost; oil and gas leasing off New England remains governed by the ordinary leasing process, which a future administration could open, while the bill's supporters have nothing to show beyond cosponsorship. The outcome so far favors whichever industry or administration wants the option to drill kept alive.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drilling option remains open; nothing locked in

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is regional rather than partisan: all 12 New England senators support it, including 8 of 45 Senate Democrats, 1 of 55 Republicans (Sen. Collins), and 1 of 2 Independents (Sen. King).

industries.note: The bill permanently removes New England's federal waters from the leasing map, eliminating any future drilling option there. Drilling in these waters would put regional fishing and tourism economies at risk from spills, so the industry's interest in opening them runs against what the bill's coastal constituents want.

industries.industry: New England commercial fishing and seafood
industries.note: A permanent ban removes the risk that drilling platforms, seismic surveying, or a spill would disrupt fisheries and close waters that span multiple states. Fishing is an established industry that cannot relocate if its grounds are damaged.
Beach and coastal tourism economies depend on clean water and shorelines; a statutory ban lowers the long-term risk of spills and offshore industrialization in their viewshed.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, whose chair has not scheduled a hearing or markup. Single-sponsor regional bills of this kind rarely advance on their own; the most likely path is that it stays in committee and dies at the end of the 119th Congress unless the delegation attaches the ban to a broader bill, such as a coast guard or energy package, that must pass.
